text: Every quantum hardware announcement leads with one number — a thousand qubits — and that number is almost always the least useful thing you could know about the device. This lesson teaches you what to look at instead.

If you only read press releases, progress looks like a qubit-count race: 27, then 127, then 433, then over 1,000. It's tempting to treat that like clock speed on an old CPU box — bigger number, better chip. It doesn't work that way. A qubit that can't hold a useful state long enough, or can't be reached by the qubits it needs to interact with, contributes close to nothing to what the device can actually compute. Scaling the count of noisy objects up without controlling their quality just gives you more noise, not more computing power. A device with a thousand low-fidelity, poorly connected qubits can be less useful than one with fifty high-fidelity, well-connected ones.

Fidelity measures how close a real operation comes to its ideal mathematical version — and there isn't one fidelity number per device, there are several. Single-qubit gate fidelity is usually the highest on the chip, often 99.9 percent or better on modern devices. Two-qubit gate fidelity is almost always noticeably worse, because entangling gates require precise interaction between physical systems and are far more sensitive to crosstalk and drift. And readout fidelity — how accurately the final measurement reports the qubit's state — matters on its own: excellent gate fidelity paired with unreliable readout still delivers garbage answers.

Put qubit count, coherence, and connectivity together and you get the rule this lesson is really about: a circuit is runnable only if a device has enough qubits to hold the problem, enough coherent circuit depth to execute the full gate sequence before noise destroys it, and enough connectivity to route it without exploding that depth with SWAPs — joined by and, not or. Excellent on any two of these while weak on the third still fails. Judging a device on qubit count alone silently assumes the other two are fine, which is exactly the assumption marketing numbers let you skip past.

Next lesson introduces a benchmark that was designed specifically to fold several of these factors into a single number — Quantum Volume — because evaluating them one at a time, the way this lesson just did, is accurate but slow.
